15.title: Rebbe Nachman's practice: go outside and talk
15.hook: Rebbe Nachman's practice: go outside and talk
15.tomorrow: the day the whole people says sorry together
15.howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim, and many other Jews, practice hitbodedut by going somewhere alone, often outdoors at night, and speaking to God aloud in their own language for a set time each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kavanah, aiming your heart where your words are going. Your line was mean it. Did one autopilot phrase get meant? Day fifteen.

Picture a small town in Ukraine, a little over two hundred years ago. It's night. Out past the last houses, in a field, a man is walking alone among the grass. He isn't reading from a book. He isn't singing a set prayer. He's talking. Out loud, in plain Yiddish, the language of his kitchen, the way you'd talk to a friend you trust: about his day, his worries, what he's ashamed of, what he wants. Anyone passing might think he's lost his mind. He's doing exactly what his teacher told him to do. Today: the rabbi who sent people outside to talk.
screen: `A FIELD AT NIGHT.` → `A MAN TALKING OUT LOUD.` → `NO BOOK, NO SET WORDS.`

segments.voice: The teacher was Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, who lived from 1772 to 1810, a great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidism. The practice is called hitbodedut, from a Hebrew root that means alone. Making yourself alone. Rebbe Nachman taught that besides the fixed prayers, the ones in the prayer book, a person should set aside time every day, an hour if possible, to speak to God in their own words and their own language. Not Hebrew, if Hebrew isn't how you talk. Whatever language your heart actually uses. Best of all in a field or a forest, among the grass, where, he said, every blade joins in. And he was practical about the hard days. If you can't find anything to say, he taught, then say that. Tell God you can't find the words. Even repeating one phrase, over and over, like master of the world, counts. The point isn't eloquence. The point is showing up and opening your mouth. He found the idea in the Torah. In Genesis, Isaac, Abraham's son, is described this way in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." The rabbis read that as Isaac praying, outside, at the end of the day. Breslov Hasidim still practice hitbodedut, often at night, often outdoors, and many other Jews have taken it up too. It sits right next to yesterday's word. The fixed prayers give you words to mean. Hitbodedut asks you to mean words that are entirely your own.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, and this one uses your voice. If you can, speak out loud, even in a whisper. If you pray, talk to God the way Rebbe Nachman taught: plainly, in your own words, about whatever is actually on your mind. If you don't pray, say out loud what's on your mind anyway, as if to a friend who's listening. If nothing comes, say that nothing comes. The bell holds the time.
Hitbodedut. Making yourself alone, to talk to God out loud in your own words. Fifteenth word.
Your line: talk to him out loud. Today, find five minutes alone, a walk, a car, a quiet room, and speak what's on your heart, out loud, in your own words. Day fifteen.

16.title: the day the whole people says sorry together
16.hook: the day the whole people says sorry together
16.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur Jews fast for about twenty-five hours, many wear white and no leather shoes, and spend much of the day in synagogue, from Kol Nidre in the evening to Neilah and the final shofar blast at nightfall; in the days before, many ask forgiveness of people they have wronged.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hitbodedut, going off alone to talk out loud in your own words. Your line was talk to him out loud. Did you find five minutes to speak? Day sixteen.

It's the evening of the holiest day of the Jewish year, and the synagogue is fuller than it's been all year. People who haven't come since last autumn are here. Many are dressed in white. Some are wearing sneakers under their good clothes. Nobody has eaten since before sunset, and nobody will until the stars come out tomorrow night. Then a cantor begins a melody so old and so familiar that some people cry before a word is sung, and it's sung three times, each time a little louder. For the next twenty-five hours, a whole people will say sorry, together. Today: Yom Kippur.
screen: `THE FULLEST NIGHT OF THE YEAR.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, NO FOOD.` → `A MELODY SUNG THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the day of atonement. The Torah sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the autumn, and tells the people to afflict their souls, which the rabbis understood as a fast. So for about twenty-five hours: no food, no water, no leather shoes, no washing for pleasure. Many wear white, like angels, some say, who don't need to eat. The evening begins with Kol Nidre, the melody from the start. And then the confessions. Here's what surprises people. They're in the plural. Not I have sinned. We have. One confession runs through the Hebrew alphabet, a sin for every letter, and everyone says every line, lightly tapping their chest, including lines about things they personally never did. The whole community stands together as one. Nobody is singled out, and nobody gets to pretend they're above it. But the day has a limit, and the rabbis wrote it down plainly. The Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for what's between a person and God. For what's between you and another person, it doesn't, until you've made it right with them. So in the days before, Jews call each other, write, knock on doors, and ask forgiveness. The fast doesn't replace the phone call. In the afternoon, the book of Jonah is read, a story about a whole city that turns around and is given another chance. And as the sun goes down, the last service is called Neilah, the closing of the gates. The doors of the ark stay open, the room stands, and at nightfall one long blast of the ram's horn ends it. Then everybody goes home and eats.

17.title: return, not repentance
17.hook: return, not repentance — you're not lost, you're facing the wrong way
17.tomorrow: why some prayers need ten people
17.howItsDone: Jews focus on teshuvah especially in the month of Elul and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, reflecting on the year, apologizing to people they've wronged and resolving to change, though tradition holds it's possible any day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yom Kippur, a whole people saying sorry together. Your line was you can start over. Did you take one step toward that apology? Day seventeen.

You're driving somewhere new, and you miss the exit. The map on your phone doesn't lecture you. It doesn't tell you you're a bad driver or that you've ruined the trip. It just says: recalculating. And then, somewhere up ahead: make a U-turn. You were never lost, exactly. You were going the wrong way, and the way back was always there. English has a heavy word for what happens after we do wrong: repentance. It sounds like sackcloth and shame. The Hebrew word underneath it is much closer to that voice on the map. Today: teshuvah.

Teshuvah comes from shuv, to turn, to return. It doesn't say you're broken. It says you're facing the wrong way, and you can turn around. The prophet Hosea calls out, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Return. As if home were still there, and it is. The same Hebrew word also means an answer, a reply. Turning around is answering a call. The rabbis thought teshuvah was so basic to the world that they listed it among the things created before the world itself, before anyone had done anything wrong. The way back was built before the road. So how does a person actually turn? Maimonides, in his laws of teshuvah, lays it out plainly. Stop doing the thing. Regret it, honestly. Say it out loud, in words, not just in your head. And decide not to do it again. And then his test for complete teshuvah: you find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation and the same strength, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't. Because you've turned. There are two bold teachings about where this leads. One says: in the place where a person who has returned stands, even the completely righteous cannot stand. The one who turned has walked a road the others never had to walk. And another says that when teshuvah comes from love, even deliberate wrongs are transformed into merits, as if the wrong turn became part of the way home. The whole month before the new year, and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, are set aside for exactly this. But the door isn't only open in autumn. It's open today.

18.title: why some prayers need ten people
18.hook: why some prayers need ten people
18.howItsDone: Jewish communities gather a minyan of ten for daily and Sabbath services so that the Torah can be read and Barchu and Kaddish said; Orthodox communities count ten men, while Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist communities count women and men alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday: teshuvah, turning around, not drowning in shame. Your line was turn around. Did you make one small U-turn? Day eighteen.

It's seven in the morning on a weekday, and a man is standing at the door of a small synagogue, looking up and down the street. Inside, eight people are waiting. He counts them again. Eight, nine with him. Then a stranger walks past with a coffee, and the man calls out, a little embarrassed: excuse me, are you Jewish? Do you have ten minutes? We need one more. Stories like this happen all over the world, every morning. People have missed trains to be the tenth. Today: why some prayers can't be said until there are ten.
screen: `SEVEN IN THE MORNING.` → `EIGHT, NINE.` → `WE NEED ONE MORE.`

segments.voice: A minyan is a count: ten adults, the smallest number Jewish law calls a community. A person can pray alone, anywhere, and Jews do. But certain prayers, the ones that speak as a public, need the ten. The call to prayer, Barchu. The reading of the Torah from the scroll. And the Kaddish, including the mourner's Kaddish, said by someone who has lost a parent or a close relative. Why ten? The rabbis found it in the Torah, in a roundabout way. When the twelve spies return from the promised land, ten of them bring back a frightening report, and God calls those ten a congregation. So the rabbis said: ten make a congregation. Some teachers also point back to day eight, when Abraham bargained for Sodom and stopped at ten. Ten was the smallest number that could save a city. Who counts toward the ten is something Jews answer differently. In Orthodox communities, the minyan is ten men over the age of thirteen. In Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist communities, women count equally. Now think about what the rule does for a mourner. For eleven months after a parent dies, a traditional mourner says Kaddish every day. And because it needs a minyan, they can't say it alone. Every single day, nine other people have to show up for them, and answer amen. The rule makes sure grief is never carried in an empty room. There's an old teaching that when ten gather to pray, the divine presence is among them. And ask anyone who's been the tenth, the stranger pulled in off the street: it feels good to be the one who made it count.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Count your own minyan. Think of the people who would show up if you called: at a hospital, at a funeral, at a table. Name them in your head, one at a time, and see how far you get. Ten, or three, or one. Then think of someone who might not reach ten, and whose count you could join. The bell holds the time.
Minyan. A count of ten, the smallest community, so some prayers are never said alone. Eighteenth word.

19.title: the words on the doorpost
19.hook: the words on the doorpost; touching it on the way out
19.howItsDone: Jews fix a mezuzah, a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages in a case, on the right doorpost of the home's doorways, and many touch it and kiss their fingers when passing through.

segments.voice: Yesterday: minyan, the count of ten so no mourner prays alone. Your line was some things need company. Were you someone's tenth? Day nineteen.

Next time you're in a Jewish friend's home, or a Jewish-owned shop, look at the right side of the front door, about shoulder height. There's often a small narrow case, wood or metal or ceramic, fixed to the frame at a slight angle. Watch people go in and out. Some walk right past it. Some reach up, touch it with their fingertips, and then touch their fingers to their lips, without breaking stride, the way you'd pat your pocket for your keys. It takes a second. Most people outside the tradition think the little case is the point. It isn't. Today: what's inside.
screen: `THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE DOOR.` → `A SMALL CASE, SLIGHTLY TILTED.` → `FINGERTIPS, THEN LIPS.`

segments.voice: Mezuzah just means doorpost. The commandment is right after the Shema, the six words from day two. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And thou shalt write them upon the door-posts of thy house, and upon thy gates." So Jews did, literally. Inside the case is a small piece of parchment, handwritten by a trained scribe with a quill and special ink, carrying the Shema and the passages around it. The case is just a case. The words are the mezuzah. It's rolled up, and on the back is often written one of God's names, Shaddai, which many read as the initials of guardian of the doors of Israel. Now the tilt. The medieval commentator Rashi said the mezuzah should hang upright. His grandson, Rabbeinu Tam, said it should lie flat. Two great teachers, one doorpost. Ashkenazi Jews, from central and eastern Europe, settled it by hanging it at an angle, a little of both. Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright. So every tilted mezuzah is a small monument to an argument nobody lost. The parchment is checked by a scribe twice every seven years, because a faded letter makes it unfit. And it goes on nearly every doorway in the home, not just the front door, though never the bathroom. Why touch it? Maimonides warned against treating it as a lucky charm. It's a reminder. Every time you cross a threshold, going out into the world or coming home from it, you pass the words: hear, love, teach them to your children, speak of them when you walk by the way. The touch says: I'm taking these with me.

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Picture the front door of your home. The frame, the handle, the way the light falls there. The mezuzah. The doorpost, and the handwritten words of the Shema rolled up and fixed there. Nineteenth word.
Your line: take the words with you. Today, every time you walk through a doorway, touch the frame and remember the one thing you chose to carry. Day nineteen.

20.title: not a book
20.hook: not a book — a scroll, hand-written, read to the end and rolled back
20.howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah scroll is taken from the ark, carried through the congregation, and read aloud in a set portion each Sabbath, finishing and beginning again each year on Simchat Torah with singing and dancing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mezuzah, handwritten words on the doorpost. Your line was take the words with you. Did a doorway remind you? Day twenty.
screen: `THE MEZUZAH — TAKE THE WORDS WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Imagine a book that nobody is allowed to print. Every copy has to be written by hand, letter by letter, with a feather, on animal skin, by someone trained for years. One copy takes about a year. If a single letter is missing, or two letters touch, the whole thing can't be used until it's fixed. Nobody touches the writing with their fingers; they follow it with a silver pointer. When it's carried through a room, people stand, and some reach out to kiss it. When one is too old to use, it's buried like a person. Today: the scroll at the center of Jewish life.
screen: `A BOOK NOBODY CAN PRINT.` → `A YEAR TO WRITE ONE COPY.` → `CARRIED, KISSED, BURIED.`

segments.voice: Torah comes from a Hebrew root that means to aim, to point, to teach. Torah is teaching, instruction, the way pointed out. In its narrowest sense, it's the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written in a scroll by a scribe called a sofer. Something over three hundred thousand letters, every one counted. Wider, Torah means the whole of the Hebrew Bible. Wider still, all of Jewish teaching, down to a good answer given at a kitchen table last night. The Psalms describe it, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation, like this: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. A lamp, enough for the next step. Here's the part that makes it different from a book on a shelf. The scroll is read, in public, from beginning to end, one section each week, over a year. And on the autumn festival called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, the reader finishes the last lines of Deuteronomy, and immediately, without a pause, rolls the whole scroll back and starts again with Genesis. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The story is never finished. There's a well-known teaching about the letters, too. The Torah ends with the letter lamed and begins with the letter bet. Put the end next to the beginning, and they spell lev, heart. The scroll runs in a circle, and the circle is a heart. So the Torah isn't a book you finish. It's a book a whole people reads together, at the same pace, year after year, for more than two thousand years.

One sentence. Say it to yourself slowly, like a scribe copying it one letter at a time. Then ask where it's pointing you next. The bell holds the time.
Torah. Teaching: a handwritten scroll, read from end back to beginning, year after year. Twentieth word.
Your line: the world's oldest book club. Today, share one line you love with someone else, the way a whole people shares one scroll. Day twenty.

21.carry: join the cycle wherever it is
21.howItsDone: Jews read the weekly Torah portion aloud from the scroll in synagogue on Sabbath mornings, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings and Sabbath afternoons, and many study it at home during the week.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Torah, the handwritten scroll, read to the end and rolled back. Your line was the world's oldest book club. Did you share a line you love? Day twenty-one, the last day of camp one.

This Saturday morning, in a synagogue in Buenos Aires, one in Melbourne, one in a Brooklyn basement and one in a Jerusalem neighborhood, the scroll will be opened to the same place. The same chapters, read in the same week, in the same order, by people who will never meet. Ask a Jewish friend what this week's portion is, and there's a good chance they'll know its name without checking. It's a calendar made of text. And as camp one ends, it's also the road ahead of you on this path. Today: the portion, and where it's about to take us.
screen: `ONE SATURDAY, EVERY CITY.` → `THE SAME CHAPTERS, THE SAME WEEK.` → `A CALENDAR MADE OF TEXT.`

segments.voice: A parsha is a portion. The five books of the Torah are divided into fifty-four of them, and one is read each Sabbath, so the whole scroll is read in about a year. There are fewer Sabbaths than portions in some years, so some weeks two are read together. Each portion is named for one of its first distinctive words. The first is Bereshit, in the beginning. Then Noach, Noah. Then Lech Lecha, go forth, when Abraham leaves home. Jews say the week's name the way other people say the month: that happened the week of Noach. The reading isn't only on Saturday morning. Short pieces are read on Monday and Thursday mornings too, and tradition credits the scribe Ezra with that custom, so that no one would go three days without Torah. The Talmud even suggests a way to study it at home: read the week's portion twice, and once in translation. And here's a detail that says a lot about a scattered people. After some holidays, Israel and the rest of the world fall out of step by a week, and then quietly catch up again. The cycle bends, but it holds. That's why the carry for today is what it is. You don't start the Torah on page one when you're ready. You find out where everyone is, and you step in there. Camp one gave you twenty-one words. Tomorrow camp two begins, the stories, the original serial, and it begins exactly where the cycle does: at the first word, Bereshit.
screen: `FIFTY-FOUR PORTIONS, ONE A WEEK.` · `EACH NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.` · `MONDAY, THURSDAY, SABBATH.` · `THE CYCLE BENDS, BUT HOLDS.` · then, large: `STEP IN WHERE EVERYONE IS.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell, to walk back through camp one. Let the words come one by one: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, the candles, bracha, Genesis one, the Sabbath commandment. Abraham, Jacob, tzedakah, the Exodus, Sinai, the Ten Words, kavanah. Hitbodedut, Yom Kippur, teshuvah, minyan, the mezuzah, Torah, the parsha. Stay with whichever one pulls at you. The bell holds the time.
The parsha. This week's portion, one of fifty-four, read by a whole people in step. Twenty-first word. Camp one, complete.
Your line: join the cycle wherever it is. Today, look up this week's portion and read its first few lines, wherever the year happens to be. Tomorrow, the stories begin. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `CAMP ONE COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: BEFORE ANYTHING, A VOICE.`

trapdoor: what you thought: a reading assignment.
what it means: a calendar made of text. one of fifty-four portions, read by the whole people in the same week.
what a scholar hears: Bava Kamma 82a credits Ezra with the Monday and Thursday readings; Berakhot 8a: read the portion twice and the Targum once. Israel and the diaspora sometimes run a week apart.
